title: cos(40°) = cos(2π/9) and the Triple-Angle Framework
content: The polynomial 8X³−6X+1 is the minimal polynomial of cos(40°) = cos(2π/9) over ℚ. The three roots are cos(40°), cos(80°), cos(160°). The file header explains the key algebraic identity: β = 2α²−1 comes from the double-angle formula cos(80°) = 2cos²(40°)−1, and γ = −α−β from Vieta's formula (the X² coefficient is 0, so α+β+γ = 0). The Eisenstein substitution Y=2X−2 (not Y=2X+2 as for the cos(20°) case) reflects the +1 vs −1 constant term in the polynomial.
mathContext: The polynomial $8X^3 - 6X + c$ with $c = \pm 1$ arises from the triple-angle formula: $\cos(3\theta) = 4\cos^3(\theta) - 3\cos(\theta)$. Setting $4\cos^3(\theta) - 3\cos(\theta) = \pm 1/2$ (i.e., $\cos(3\theta) = \pm 1/2$) gives $8\cos^3(\theta) - 6\cos(\theta) \mp 1 = 0$. For $\theta = 40°$: $\cos(120°) = -1/2$, giving $8X^3-6X+1=0$. For $\theta = 20°$: $\cos(60°) = 1/2$, giving $8X^3-6X-1=0$. The three roots of $8X^3-6X+1$ are $\{\cos(40°), \cos(80°), \cos(160°)\}$, the values $\cos(2k\pi/9)$ for $k=1,2,4$.

title: Root Images via Ring Identities: β and γ in Any Commutative Ring
content: The theorems `root_image_beta` and `root_image_gamma` work in any CommRing R, not just ℝ or ℚ. Given 8a³−6a+1 = 0, the identities factor as: 8(2a²−1)³−6(2a²−1)+1 = (8a³−6a−1)(8a³−6a+1), so the factor containing the hypothesis (= 0) kills the expression. The `ring` tactic proves the factored form, then `mul_zero` finishes. This abstraction is crucial: the same identities work in the splitting field ℝ (for the geometric interpretation) and in abstract polynomial quotient rings.
mathContext: The algebraic magic: $8(2\alpha^2-1)^3 - 6(2\alpha^2-1) + 1 = (8\alpha^3 - 6\alpha - 1)(8\alpha^3 - 6\alpha + 1)$. When $8\alpha^3 - 6\alpha + 1 = 0$, the right side $= (8\alpha^3 - 6\alpha - 1) \cdot 0 = 0$. This ring identity is the formal version of the geometric fact that the double-angle formula sends cos(40°) to cos(80°). For $\gamma = -2\alpha^2 - \alpha + 1$: the cofactor is $(-8\alpha^3 - 12\alpha^2 + 3)$, derived from $\gamma = -(\alpha + \beta)$ via Vieta ($\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 0$ since the $X^2$ coefficient is 0).

title: Eisenstein Irreducibility: The Shift Y = 2X − 2
content: The polynomial 8X³−6X+1 is not directly Eisenstein (no prime divides all non-leading coefficients — 8 is not divisible by 3, and 1 is not). The key is the substitution Y=2X−2 (solving for X=(Y+2)/2): substituting X=(Y+2)/2 into 8X³−6X+1 gives Y³+6Y²+9Y+3. This polynomial IS Eisenstein at p=3: 3|6, 3|9, 3|3, but 9∤3. By Gauss's lemma, irreducibility over ℤ implies irreducibility over ℚ. The map X ↦ (Y+2)/2 is an isomorphism of polynomial rings.
mathContext:
Eisenstein's criterion: If $f = a_n X^n + \ldots + a_0 \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ with $p 
mid a_n$, $p \mid a_i$ for $i < n$, and $p^2 
mid a_0$, then $f$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$. For $r = Y^3 + 6Y^2 + 9Y + 3$ with $p=3$: $3 
mid 1$, $3 \mid 6$, $3 \mid 9$, $3 \mid 3$, $9 
mid 3$. ✓. The relationship: $r(Y) = 8(Y/2 + 1)^3 - 6(Y/2 + 1) + 1$, equivalently $r(2X-2) = 8X^3-6X+1$. Contrast: for cos(20°) polynomial $8X^3-6X-1$, the shift is $Y=2X+2$ (note $+2$ vs $-2$), giving $Y^3-6Y^2+9Y-3$, Eisenstein at 3 with all negative signs.

title: Splitting Field Degree 3: All Roots in ℚ(α)
content: The key step for proving |Gal| = 3 is showing [SplittingField:ℚ] = 3. Since 8X³−6X+1 is irreducible of degree 3, [ℚ(α):ℚ] = 3. The theorem `adjoin_root_eq_top` shows the splitting field equals ℚ(α): all three roots (α, β=2α²−1, γ=−2α²−α+1) are in ℚ(α). This uses the factored form identity: 8a³−6a+1 = 8(a−α)(a−β)(a−γ) when 8α³−6α+1=0. The equality of splitting field with ℚ(α) is established by showing the root set generates ℚ(α).
mathContext: The factored form: $8a^3-6a+1 = 8(a-\alpha)(a-\beta)(a-\gamma)$ when $\alpha$ is a root. This can be verified by checking that $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are roots (proved in Part I) and that $8(a-\alpha)(a-\beta)(a-\gamma)$ has leading coefficient 8 and constant term $8(-\alpha)(-\beta)(-\gamma) = -8\alpha\beta\gamma$. The splitting field $\text{SF} = \mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ since both $\beta, \gamma \in \mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$. By the tower law and $[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] = 3$ (from irreducibility), $[\text{SF}:\mathbb{Q}] = 3$.

title: cos40_gal_card: The Galois Group Has Order 3
content: The main theorem `cos40_gal_card` proves |Gal(8X³−6X+1/ℚ)| = 3 in two steps: first `Polynomial.Gal.card_of_separable` gives |Gal| = [SplittingField:ℚ], then `splitting_finrank` gives [SplittingField:ℚ] = 3. The separability follows from characteristic 0 (ℚ has char 0, and `Polynomial.Gal.card_of_separable` applies to separable polynomials). Together with AngleTrisectionCos20Gal (cos(20°) case, |Gal|=3) and the cos(π/7) case, this establishes that all three classical cubic angle-trisection polynomials have Galois group of order 3 (cyclic group ℤ/3ℤ).
mathContext: The Galois group of $p$ over $\mathbb{Q}$: $|\text{Gal}(p)| = [\text{SplittingField}(p):\mathbb{Q}] = 3$. Since $|\text{Gal}| = 3$ is prime, $\text{Gal} \cong \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ (the unique group of order 3). This is a cyclic group, which implies the extension $\mathbb{Q}(\cos(40°))/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois with cyclic Galois group. Galois correspondence: the only subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ are $\{0\}$ and $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$, giving only $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{Q}(\cos(40°))$ as intermediate fields. The non-constructibility of the 40° trisection follows: constructible numbers live in extensions of degree a power of 2, but $[\mathbb{Q}(\cos(40°)):\mathbb{Q}] = 3$.
